# Swift & runtime development notes

> Swift language notes, Objective-C messaging, KVO, blocks and code organisation.

## Historical context

Historical development notes from 2015–2017. Their original publication dates and source attribution are retained; translation or catalog updates do not make the examples current.
The examples were not rerun for this reorganization. Old Swift syntax, APIs, dependencies, service addresses and App Store rules may be obsolete; check current official documentation before applying them.

## Articles by original publication date

- [Objective-C runtime fundamentals: properties and instance variables](https://allluckly.cn/en/journal/2016-01-10-objective-c-runtime-fundamentals-properties-and-instance-variables/index.md): Distinguishes Objective-C properties from instance variables, examining runtime structures, memory offsets and synthesize to explain how properties are generated. Examples then show why dynamically inspecting and manipulating an object's structure can be useful. Originally published: 2016-01-10. Originally credited to SindriLin; edited and archived by Bison.
- [Inside KVO on iOS](https://allluckly.cn/en/journal/2016-01-16-inside-kvo-on-ios/index.md): Starts with observing a list's scroll offset, then examines the dynamic subclass and isa-pointer changes caused by registering an observer. Runtime functions are used to attempt a similar mechanism, connecting practical KVO usage with its underlying behaviour. Originally published: 2016-01-16. Originally credited to SindriLin; edited and archived by Bison.
- [Seven Swift pitfalls and how to avoid them](https://allluckly.cn/en/journal/2016-02-16-seven-swift-pitfalls-and-how-to-avoid-them/index.md): Uses code examples to investigate surprising behaviour in protocol extensions, optional-chain assignment and functional processing. It compares dispatch for value and reference types and explains how code can compile successfully while producing an unexpected result. Originally published: 2016-02-16. Published in 2016. Interpret the language behaviour and examples in the context of the Swift version used then. Originally credited to bestswifter; edited and archived by Bison.
- [iOS refactoring notes: Extract Method](https://allluckly.cn/en/journal/2016-03-01-ios-refactoring-notes-extract-method/index.md): Applies the Extract Method technique from Refactoring to split long stretches of code into functions organised by intent. Parameters, local variables and return values are handled step by step, with examples showing how to reduce repetition and improve readability. Originally published: 2016-03-01. Originally credited to SindriLin; edited and archived by Bison.
- [Understanding blocks in iOS development](https://allluckly.cn/en/journal/2016-04-06-understanding-blocks-in-ios-development/index.md): Starts with block declarations and calls, then examines captured variables and callback wrappers. Examples modelled on Swift's higher-order functions demonstrate how blocks can be used to process data in Objective-C. Originally published: 2016-04-06. Originally credited to Sindri; edited and archived by Bison.
- [Objective-C runtime in practice: changing fonts throughout an interface](https://allluckly.cn/en/journal/2016-05-04-objective-c-runtime-in-practice-changing-fonts-throughout-an-interface/index.md): Starts with registering a custom font and finding its name, then uses Objective-C runtime techniques to replace interface fonts. It discusses the differences between controls created in code and those loaded from a storyboard when applying a common setting. Originally published: 2016-05-04. Originally credited to HenryCheng; edited and archived by Bison.
- [Reading the Objective-C runtime source to understand messaging](https://allluckly.cn/en/journal/2016-05-20-reading-the-objective-c-runtime-source-to-understand-messaging/index.md): Uses an unrecognized selector error to introduce Objective-C messaging, examining method lookup, caching and forwarding in the source. Runtime examples then explain how a method call is resolved during execution. Originally published: 2016-05-20. Published in 2016. Source structure and implementation details refer to the Objective-C runtime of that period. Originally credited to Sindri; edited and archived by Bison.
- [Swift in practice: the template pattern](https://allluckly.cn/en/journal/2016-06-29-swift-in-practice-the-template-pattern/index.md): Uses product data and calculations to examine code that depends on a tuple's structure. Types and protocols then organise reusable processing, showing how abstraction can reduce coupling between parameter formats and business methods. Originally published: 2016-06-29. Originally credited to Sindri; edited and archived by Bison.
- [Decoupling iOS Views from Concrete Model Types](https://allluckly.cn/en/journal/2016-07-28-decoupling-ios-views-from-concrete-model-types/index.md): Uses several types of ticket data with different fields but similar presentation needs to explore a dictionary-backed approach. A protocol exposes common display properties, reducing cells' and controllers' dependence on specific models and clarifying where data conversion belongs. Originally published: 2016-07-28. Originally credited to Sindri; edited and archived by Bison.
- [Objective-C Runtime in Practice: Mapping Dictionaries to Models](https://allluckly.cn/en/journal/2016-08-16-objective-c-runtime-in-practice-mapping-dictionaries-to-models/index.md): Moves from manual assignment, KVC, and third-party model libraries to an NSObject category that traverses runtime information and maps dictionaries to models. It also defines the example's support for two levels of nested data. Originally published: 2016-08-16. Originally credited to Bison. Content is retained as published.
- [Protocols and Delegation in iOS](https://allluckly.cn/en/journal/2016-09-01-protocols-and-delegation-in-ios/index.md): Uses UITableView and custom controls to distinguish protocols from delegation. It compares delegate and block callbacks, then discusses how data sources and protocol abstractions can reduce coupling between objects. Originally published: 2016-09-01. Originally credited to Sindri; edited and archived by Bison.
- [Swift 3.0 Design Patterns: Flyweight](https://allluckly.cn/en/journal/2016-10-13-swift-3-0-design-patterns-flyweight/index.md): Introduces the flyweight pattern through shared local-data managers. A dictionary reuses loaded data and tracks usage counts; unused data is saved and released. The example contrasts this lifecycle with a singleton that remains in memory. Originally published: 2016-10-13. The title explicitly places this design-pattern tutorial in the context of Swift 3.0. Originally credited to Sindri; edited and archived by Bison.
- [Swift 3.0 Design Patterns: Singleton](https://allluckly.cn/en/journal/2016-10-13-swift-3-0-design-patterns-singleton/index.md): Introduces the uses and trade-offs of Swift singletons, creating shared instances with a static class constant or a global constant. It covers private initializers, access across modules, and the need to consider thread safety for shared mutable state. Originally published: 2016-10-13. The article explicitly discusses singleton syntax after Swift 3.0 and changes to the dispatch_once API. Originally credited to Sindri; edited and archived by Bison.
- [Balancing Code Responsibilities in iOS](https://allluckly.cn/en/journal/2016-10-27-balancing-code-responsibilities-in-ios/index.md): Uses an example project to examine oversized MVC controllers and the responsibilities of views, models, and controllers. It extracts repeated logic and reassigns functionality, emphasizing clear ownership of code before switching architecture labels. Originally published: 2016-10-27. Originally credited to Sindri; edited and archived by Bison.
- [Bitwise Operations in iOS](https://allluckly.cn/en/journal/2016-11-07-bitwise-operations-in-ios/index.md): Introduces bitwise AND, OR, XOR, and NOT, using packed RGBA colors and state flags as examples. It then explains how enumerations and masks can store and query several states together. Originally published: 2016-11-07. Originally credited to Sindri; edited and archived by Bison.
